title: Computational complexity of heat exchanger network synthesis
contribution: Proves that heat exchanger network synthesis is NP-hard in the strong sense: the minimum-number-of-matches target, restricted to one temperature interval with unit costs and equal sink demands, is equivalent to 3-PARTITION, and every published vertical-matches and simultaneous MINLP formulation contains it, while the minimum utilities targets are in P.
problem_entry: Forty years and 300+ papers on HENS but no complexity study, and process-synthesis subproblems generally unclassified (Ahmed & Sahinidis the only exception); entered by classifying each published formulation by its source (pp. 2-3, 27).
key_idea: Restrict the Papoulias-Grossmann matches model to K = 1, unit costs, 3n sources in (B/4, B/2) and n sinks of demand B, prove equivalence with 3-PARTITION, then reduce VM, EVM, MN, UMN and S to this core by zeroing weights and removing constraints that become redundant; utilities targets are network flows in P; an appendix gives an ordinary NP-hardness proof via knapsack (pp. 7, 10-25, 36-38).
assumptions: P != NP (p. 3); supply-demand balance from the prior utilities problem (p. 8); the hard instance read physically as one interval, equal cold-stream heat, no cost difference between matches (p. 10); simultaneous models inherit interval partitioning or isothermal mixing, no split stream through more than one exchanger and no by-passes (pp. 17, 19, 21); restrictions Nmax = |I|+|J|+1, beta_ij = 0, zero utility and area costs, one stage (pp. 18, 21, 23-24).
proof_devices: Restriction to 3-PARTITION via a bipartite match graph; the size window B/4 < s_i < B/2 forces three unsplit sources per sink (Theorem 2, pp. 11-12)
Decision version first, strong NP-completeness carried to the optimization problems (Corollaries 1-3, pp. 10, 12)
Redundancy after restriction: constraint blocks whose variables leave the objective are removed ((7), (11) p. 14; (16), (19) pp. 24-25)
Literature feasibility theorem (Floudas et al.: every feasible match set admits a network) used to drop the network constraints (Theorem 3, p. 18)
Polynomial subproblem solved inside the reduction: utility loads from problem U fixed as bounds, utility binaries forced to 1 (Theorem 4, p. 21)
Membership in P by recognizing a min-cost network flow (strongly polynomial) and an LP (Khachian) (Theorem 1, p. 7)
Knapsack equivalence completed by a transportation problem made feasible by the Northwest Corner rule (Theorem 6, pp. 37-38)
positioning: Classifies, without criticizing, the published formulations of Papoulias-Grossmann, Cerda-Westerberg, Gundersen-Grossmann, Gundersen et al., Floudas-Ciric, Ciric-Floudas and Yee-Grossmann; complexity theory from Garey-Johnson and Papadimitriou-Steiglitz; the only process-systems predecessor named is his group's planning complexity paper (pp. 2-3, 5, 27).
writing: Abstract concedes the result 'may not be surprising', then stresses the strong sense and the simplicity of the hard subproblems; a two-page complexity primer for chemical engineers; formulation-restriction-theorem rhythm; summary table and reduction map; the conclusion turns hardness into a pointer to heuristics (pp. 1, 3-4, 25-27, 36).
limits_future: No limits section; an efficient exact algorithm 'highly unlikely'; approximability and the network-derivation problem N not classified; future: heuristics from 3-PARTITION and Knapsack, exact and approximate algorithms exploiting Knapsack-like structure (pp. 25, 27, 36).

method_links.note: Enters the area by surveying everything that exists before any own method: every published formulation classified (ten rows) beside an annotated bibliography of 300+ papers; the instrument is a complexity classification instead of a computational benchmark.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: complexity before algorithms, then bounded heuristics
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Strong NP-hardness of every published HENS formulation, followed by pointers to heuristics from 3-PARTITION and Knapsack and to exact and approximate algorithms; S002 p. 18 describes the same programme as polynomial-time heuristics with analytically derived quality bounds (the 'science of heuristics' line).

transferable: Strong NP-hardness of a fixed-charge transshipment or transportation model: restrict to one period, unit fixed costs, 3n supplies in (B/4, B/2) and n demands of B, and prove equivalence with 3-PARTITION by counting arcs in the bipartite match graph (pp. 10-12)
Carry one hardness proof across a literature: zero the extra cost weights, fix one stage or interval, and show the remaining constraints are redundant for the restricted objective (pp. 14-25)
Drop a constraint block in a reduction by citing a feasibility theorem, and fix polynomially solvable subproblems (utilities as a network flow) before reducing (pp. 18, 21)
Summarize a classification as a table of problem, target, source and complexity plus a reduction map (pp. 26-27)
Keep a weaker hardness proof when its source problem (Knapsack) suggests algorithms, and say why (p. 36)

quotes.text: While HENS has received so much attention by the process systems engineering community, there have been no studies of its computational complexity and it is not known whether efficient (polynomial) algorithms might exist for the problem.
The proofs suggest that heuristic algorithms that have performed well for the 3-PARTITION and the Knapsack may be found useful when extended to HENS.

title: Optimization under uncertainty: state-of-the-art and opportunities
contribution: A sole-authored short review that contrasts recourse-based, robust and chance-constrained stochastic programming, fuzzy programming and stochastic dynamic programming, reports the computational state and the contributions of process systems engineering, and argues with two small examples that many problems under uncertainty are hidden multi-extremal global-optimization problems.
problem_entry: Uncertainty in prices, availability and demand; a huge uncertainty space and integer decisions in multi-stage settings make models very large; set up as a short overview with pointers to the literature and entered by contrasting modeling philosophies (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: A taxonomy by modeling philosophy with one standard formulation each, critique by guarantee and implementation status, and then the argument of section 7: seemingly linear stochastic integer and chance-constrained programs are multi-extremal or nonconvex, so global optimization is needed (pp. 3-21).
assumptions: Two-stage SLP with polyhedral sets on a probability space; discrete distributions give deterministic equivalents, continuous ones need sampling and probabilistic convergence; risk-neutral recourse vs variability-penalized robust SP; chance constraints convex under log-concavity, nonconvex in general; fuzzy linear membership functions with Bellman-Zadeh decisions; DP with Markov dynamics and additive costs (pp. 3-13).
proof_devices: Algorithms judged by guarantee and range: integer L-shaped not applicable with continuous first-stage variables, Caroe-Tind master without a practical solution method, Caroe-Schultz finite only for a discrete first stage or epsilon > 0, enumeration computationally prohibitive (pp. 5-6)

Smallest computed nonconvexity examples: EX1 with two first-stage variables and four scenarios, value function with several local minima and the global minimum at (0, 3) (pp. 19-20); EX2, a two-variable chance-constrained LP whose feasible set is the nonconvex union of two polyhedra (pp. 20-21)
Reformulations reported: Zimmermann's lambda LP for flexible programs (pp. 10-11) and the possibilistic program as a generally nonconvex NLP (p. 12)
experiments: none of its own; from the literature: exact SLPs to one million variables on parallel computers, SAA up to '1081' scenarios as extracted (probably 10^81, not checked) on a grid, only small exact SIPs, a 21694-scenario routing problem within an estimated 1%; no general-purpose fuzzy or stochastic DP software (p. 16).
positioning: Pointers to textbooks and the SP community page; criticism by guarantees and missing implementations (Higle-Sen and Sherali-Fraticelli with 'no implementations' yet, p. 6); credits process systems engineering for flexibility analysis, aggregation-disaggregation and multiparametric programming; his group's branch-and-bound, planning, bounded heuristics and global-optimization book form a recurring thread; fuzzy programming treated neutrally (pp. 2, 5-7, 11, 17-19).
writing: Pointer-style survey with one formulation, a critique and an applications list per paradigm; calibrated hedging in both directions ('It appears unlikely' for general-purpose exact algorithms, global optimization 'very likely to play a major role'); his own comparison called a small step; acknowledgments credit former students for the topics; the p. 22 follow-up sentence differs from the FOCAPO 2003 wording ('we anticipate' vs 'we expect to see') (pp. 3-16, 19, 21-22).
limits_future: Not a detailed coverage (p. 2); opportunities: systematic comparisons of modeling philosophies, the multi-stage integer case, problem-specific approximation schemes for integer and nonlinear cases, neuro-dynamic programming, global optimization for two-stage and chance-constrained models, PTAS for multi-stage programs (pp. 1, 21-22).

method_links.note: Calls for systematic comparisons between modeling philosophies, naming only his group's 1996 stochastic-vs-fuzzy study as a small step, and rates algorithms by whether implementations exist; a call and a review rather than a benchmark, and about modeling frameworks rather than solver implementations.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: complexity before algorithms, then bounded heuristics
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Own-voice description of the group's paradigm: LP-based polynomial-time heuristics whose distinguishing feature is an analytically derived quality bound, e.g. an LP-rounding and bundling scheme whose gap vanishes almost surely as the number of stages grows; the HENS approximation paper listed as submitted.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: recast a neighbouring field's models as global-optimization problems
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Section 7 shows with two smallest computed examples that seemingly linear stochastic integer and chance-constrained programs are multi-extremal or nonconvex, and proposes global optimization (Tawarmalani & Sahinidis 2002) for them.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: students as scouts into new topics
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Single own-voice instance: his former students Liu and Ahmed introduced him to many of the review's topics.

transferable: Rate each algorithm in a review by its termination guarantee, the variable types it admits and whether an implementation exists (pp. 5-6, 16)

Expose hidden nonconvexity with the smallest computed examples: a two-variable four-scenario stochastic integer program with a plotted value function, and a two-variable chance-constrained LP whose feasible set is a union of two polyhedra (pp. 19-21)
Pair a polynomial-time heuristic with an analytical quality bound (LP rounding plus bundling, gap vanishing almost surely as stages grow) and still report small-instance behaviour (pp. 18-19)
End a survey with open problems stated as gaps, each with a named first step (p. 21)

quotes.text: It appears unlikely that general-purpose algorithms will solve such problems exactly.
The distinguishing feature of this solution paradigm is the analytical derivation of bounds for the quality of the solutions obtained by heuristics that run in polynomial time.

title: Global optimization of mixed-integer nonlinear programs: A theoretical and computational study
contribution: Designs every component of branch-and-bound for factorable MINLPs (entirely LP relaxations from recursive decomposition plus a quadratically convergent sandwich rule, a Lagrangian-duality theory that derives existing range-reduction rules and two new ones, violation-transfer branching, heap-based node selection) and shows BARON solving separable concave QPs, 0-1 hyperbolic programs and MINLPLib models automatically.
problem_entry: MINLP global methods sporadic and limited to convex or quadratic cases; Remarks 1-3: B&B merely convergent in continuous spaces, dropping integrality gives no useful relaxation, NLP solvers often fail even on convex problems; B&B is a prototype whose components must be designed (pp. 2-4).
key_idea: Algorithm Relax with one auxiliary variable per subexpression and polyhedral outer approximation gives an LP relaxation; projective-error sandwich rule converges quadratically; a homogenized Lagrangian range-reduction problem (SimpleReduce) unifies optimality-, marginals-, feasibility-based reduction and probing and yields duality-based and learning reductions; violation transfer for branching; BARON implementation (pp. 4-23).
assumptions: Factorable functions with finite variable bounds implicit in every envelope; univariate library limited to monomial, power and log terms; theta < pi in Theorem 3; constraint qualifications for the comparison with the earlier cut; learning reduction needs exact representation at bounds and identical child relaxations at the branching point; absolute tolerance 1e-6 (relative 0.1 for large SCQPs) (pp. 2-3, 6-7, 11, 15, 18, 24).
proof_devices: Theorem 2: McCormick's composition (mid-function) bound implied by Algorithm Relax, via sets M, F, H in (n+2)-space, convexity under intersection and projection, and the quasiconvex envelope minimized over [c(x), C(x)] (p. 5)
Theorem 3: at most N(k) tangents for projective tolerance, k = L*theta/eps_p, by induction with Lemma 1 (ac = bd implies ac + bd <= ad + bc) and a Cauchy-Schwarz-type inequality (pp. 9-11)
Homogenizing multiplier y0 so one procedure (SimpleReduce) gives the Lagrangian bound and bounds on any constraint, with cuts reusable across nodes (pp. 12-13)
Same polyhedral cone, different normalizing planes: any dual feasible node-LP solution bounds the perturbation problem (pp. 14-15)
Theorem 4: cut g_i(x) >= (b0 - inf l(x,y))/y_i from the relaxed primal master; the Ryoo-Sahinidis 1996 cut (U - L)/y_i shown equal or weaker (p. 15)
Feasibility-based tightening rederived as Fourier-Motzkin elimination on a one-constraint LP with explicit duals (p. 16)
Sibling dual built from the fathomed child's dual by changing one multiplier; bilinear-envelope example where that multiplier increases (pp. 18-19)
Data-structure cost argument: node selection super-polynomial per node unless heaps (O(log L) insert/delete, O(1) retrieval) are used (p. 22)
experiments: One RS/6000 machine; CPU s, nodes, nodes in memory. 13 small SCQPs: general module similar nodes but about 6-23x the CPU time of the specialized module; probing cuts nodes on all 13 but raises time on 8. Large SCQPs vs GOP times published for another machine: order-of-magnitude gain only at the largest sizes, GOP96 lower on 5 of 9 parseable sizes. 0-1 hyperbolic programs vs CPLEX 6.0: BARON faster on 6 of 8, one CPLEX failure after a day. 34 selected MINLPLib models all solved, four better than the source's local solutions; no failures reported (pp. 23-27).
positioning: Earlier MINLP work convex or quadratic, recent global B&B promising (incl. own 1995); combines McCormick factorable programming with the Rote sandwich algorithm; restates nine cited range-reduction works (own included, own 1996 cut equal or weaker) as special cases; credits integer programming for marginals and probing; compares with GOP and CPLEX (pp. 2, 7-8, 15-16, 24-26).
writing: Abstract split into theoretical/algorithmic and computational parts; early contribution sentence; 'entirely automated' claim three times; proofs delegated to the thesis while the software architecture is described in the article; hedging rare (Remark 4); the text reports iteration parity of the general module but not the time ratio its own Table 1 shows (pp. 1-2, 11, 22-24, 27).
limits_future: Inline limits: simple multilinear and univariate schemes chosen to keep the implementation simple, weak sandwich bounds for small n, NP-hard Lagrangian subproblems replaced by weaker relaxations, bilinear details deferred to the thesis; the abstract's finiteness claim for certain classes has no theorem in the body; no future work stated (pp. 1, 3, 5-6, 8, 13, 20-21, 26-27).

method_links.note: Unified duality theory of range reduction; duality-based reduction re-run whenever a bound or the incumbent changes; learning reduction after fathoming; BARON's feasibility, marginals, probing and duality facilities; reduction at every node beats CPLEX on hyperbolic programs; the Ryoo-Sahinidis 1996 cut (U - L)/y_i restated and implied by Theorem 4.
Table 1 already shows the cost of probing that step 4 rations: probing lowers nodes on all 13 SCQPs but raises CPU time on 8 (not discussed in the text).
LP technology mature, NLP solvers often fail even on convex problems; nonlinear relaxations outer-approximated into an entirely LP relaxation because NLPs carry more numerical issues.

In 2004 the LP-only choice is argued, not measured (no gap-closed, time-per-node or failure counts), simplicity is the stated criterion, and the code described still builds linear/nonlinear relaxations with MINOS, SNOPT and SDPA links and a mixed-integer SDP module.
BARON as implementation of record: nine-component modular core, 12 specialized modules plus the factorable NLP module, switches and modules compared inside the code, 500+ problems in the thesis.
No BARON version named while CPLEX 6.0 is, and one comparison uses published times from another machine: the later fixed cross-paper protocol is not yet in place.

Selected MINLPLib problems from representative classes without a stated rule and no unsolved instance reported; but certified global values expose four inferior local solutions in the source of the nvs problems.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: one framework re-derives the zoo, then extends it
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The range-reduction rules of nine cited works, the authors' own 1996 cut included, become special cases of one homogenized-Lagrangian range-reduction problem, which then yields duality-based reduction from stored duals and the learning reduction.

transferable: Factorable relaxation: recursive decomposition with one auxiliary variable per distinct subexpression, McCormick envelopes for bilinear terms, recursive bilinear relaxation of products, product disaggregation for fractions, tangents for convex univariate pieces, so every node solves an LP (pp. 4-7)
Projective error rule for tangent placement (curve point closest to the intersection of the endpoint tangents), at most N(k) lines for tolerance eps_p with k = L*theta/eps_p (pp. 9-11)

Range reduction from any dual vector: g_i(x) >= (b0 - inf_x l(x,y))/y_i; store duals from dual simplex or Lagrangian iterations and re-tighten all bounds whenever a bound or the incumbent changes; tighten surrogate constraints formed with dual multipliers (pp. 15, 17)

Learning reduction: from a fathomed child with an active branching bound, derive the sibling's dual by changing only that bound's multiplier (watch bilinear-envelope switches) and cut the sibling's region (pp. 17-19)
Violation-transfer branching: propagate nonconvexity violations forward and backward through the factorable relations and weight them by marginals and priorities (pp. 19-21)
Heaps for node priority orders; store the branching decision and partition only when the node is reselected (half the memory, partial relaxation solves) (pp. 21-22)
Price generality inside one code: run the general module against your specialized module on the specialized class and report nodes and time (Table 1, p. 24)
When a global solve beats published values, check whether the source used local solutions and mark the improved entries (pp. 26-27)

quotes.text: Nonlinear programming solvers, however, often fail even in solving convex problems.

In this paper, we demonstrate that branch-and-bound is a viable tool for global optimization of purely continuous, purely integer, as well as mixed-integer nonlinear programs if supplemented with appropriate range reduction tools, relaxation schemes, and branching strategies.
